etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English brest, from Old English brēost, from Proto-West Germanic *breust, from Proto-Germanic *breustą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell”). Compare West Frisian boarst, Danish bryst, Swedish bröst; cf. also Dutch borst, German Brust.

definitions.definition: (anatomy) Either of the two organs on the front of a female human's chest, which contain the mammary glands; also the analogous organs in males.
(anatomy) The chest, or front of the human thorax.

quote.citation: 1798, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner:
quote.text: The Wedding-Guest here beat his breast, / For he heard the loud bassoon.

definitions.definition: A section of clothing covering the breast area.

quote.citation: 1956, Anthony Burgess, Time for a Tiger (The Malayan Trilogy), published 1972, page 45:
quote.text: By the time he reached the War Memorial damp had soaked through the breasts of his shirt.

definitions.definition: The figurative seat of the emotions, feelings etc.; one’s heart or innermost thoughts.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:

1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: […] Thou best know’stWhat torment I did find thee in. Thy groansDid make wolves howl, and penetrate the breastsOf ever-angry bears—it was a tormentTo lay upon the damn’d, which SycoraxCould not again undo. It was mine art,When I arrived and heard thee, that made gapeThe pine and let thee out.

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act I, page 1:
quote.text: Muſick has Charms to ſooth a ſavage Breaſt, / To ſoften Rocks, or bend a knotted Oak.

definitions.definition: The ventral portion of an animal’s thorax.
A choice cut of poultry, especially chicken or turkey, taken from the bird’s breast; also a cut of meat from other animals, breast of mutton, veal, pork.
The front or forward part of anything.

quote.citation: 2015 April 7, Jeff Howell, “The secret of longer lasting tiles [print version: How to avoid cracking up, 4 April 2015, p. P7]”, in The Daily Telegraph (Property)‎[1], archived from the original on 22 April 2015:
quote.text: If you burn wood on its own, the flue gases are cooler than from a coal fire. This can result in tars condensing out within the parging and brickwork of the flue, sometimes causing brown or yellow staining on upstairs chimney breasts.

definitions.definition: The upper surface of a landform or body of water.

quote.citation: a. 1645, John Milton, “L’Allegro”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC:
quote.text: Mountains on whose barren breast / The labouring clouds do often rest.

quote.citation: 1865, Walt Whitman, “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d”, in Sequel to Drum-Taps: When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d and other poems:
quote.text: […]  In the distance the flowing glaze, the breast of the river, with a wind-dapple here and there,  […]

definitions.definition: (mining) The face of a coal working.
(obsolete) The power of singing; a musical voice.

quote.citation: c. 1601–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Twelfe Night, or What You Will”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: By my troth, the fool has an excellent breast.

definitions.definition: (transitive, often figurative) To push against with the breast; to meet full on, oppose, face.

quote.citation: 1817, William Wirt, Sketches of the Life and Character of Patrick Henry‎[2], page 22:
quote.text: […] when the court, very much to the credit of their candour and firmness, breasted the popular current by sustaining the demurrer.

definitions.definition: To reach the top (of a hill).

quote.citation: 1947 January and February, O. S. Nock, “"The Aberdonian" in Wartime”, in Railway Magazine, page 8:
quote.text: With the sea below us grey and storm swept, and the coast line vague in the driving rain, we forged our way up the bank to breast the summit at 37 m.p.h.

quote.citation: 1960 March, Cecil J. Allen, “Locomotive Running Past and Present”, in Trains Illustrated, page 178:
quote.text: But this was excelled by the remarkable feat of Iron Duke, on the second run, in accelerating from a dead start at Miller's Dale up 1 in 90 to no less than 53 m.p.h. before breasting the summit at Peak Forest.
Breast the birds; wash and dry well. Preheat oven to 375 degrees. Place the birds in a roasting pan.
